topic: Soviet army slang 'dukhi' -- the same word for brand-new recruits and the Afghan mujahideen enemy
title: The Soviet Army Called New Recruits The Same Word As The Enemy
description: AI-narrated original commentary on Soviet military slang: how the word 'dukhi' (Russian for 'spirits'/'ghosts') was used for both brand-new conscripts under the dedovshchina hazing system and the Afghan mujahideen fighting Soviet troops during the Soviet-Afghan War. Not a reproduction or summary of any single source video.

hook_candidates.text: The Soviet army used the exact same nickname for its own rookie soldiers and the enemy trying to kill them.
What do you call a brand-new Soviet soldier and the guerrilla fighter trying to kill him? The exact same word.
New recruits weren't just hazed by their own army -- they were branded with the enemy's nickname before they even reached the front.
In the Soviet army, a brand-new recruit spent his first six months answering to the same word used for the enemy across the mountains.

contradicted_belief: Most people assume a hazed new recruit and the actual enemy would never share the same nickname, but the Soviet army gave them one.

sources.note: Confirms 'dukhi' (spirits) is the term for new Soviet conscripts in their first months under the dedovshchina hierarchy.
Confirms Soviet troops called the Afghan mujahideen 'dukhi' (ghosts) for their elusive guerrilla tactics.
Human Rights Watch documentation of the severity and systemic nature of dedovshchina hazing.

beats.text: The Soviet army used the exact **same** nickname for two totally different people.
That word was **dukhi** -- Russian for 'spirits,' or ghosts.
Brand-new conscripts got the name because for six months they had **zero** real status in the unit.
That same word -- **dukhi** -- was also what Soviet troops called the Afghan fighters trying to kill them.
Guerrillas struck from the mountains and **vanished** before anyone saw a face, so soldiers called them ghosts too.
For a lot of these teenagers, the hazing was scarier than the actual **war**.
Exact numbers are hard to pin down -- the army rarely investigated **itself**.
Same word, same war -- just depended on which side of the rifle you were **standing** on.
